statement: A minimax solution for a two-agent zero-sum game (Definition 5) requires that agent i's maxmin value equal its minmax value; every finite two-agent zero-sum normal-form game has a minimax solution (von Neumann 1928; von Neumann and Morgenstern 1944), and finite-horizon or discounted infinite-horizon two-agent zero-sum stochastic games also have minimax solutions (Shapley 1953); all minimax solutions in a game yield the same unique value to each agent.

conditions: general-sum games with n>=2 agents; finite normal-form games for the cited existence result
limits: existence for stochastic games is a separate cited result (Fink 1964; Filar and Vrieze 2012), not proved in text; a Nash equilibrium's action probabilities can be irrational for 3+ agents (Nash 1950)
statement: A Nash equilibrium (Definition 6) is a joint policy in which no agent i can improve its expected return by unilaterally deviating, holding all other agents' policies fixed (Eq. 4.16); Nash (1950) proved every finite general-sum normal-form game has at least one Nash equilibrium.

conditions: general-sum games with n agents, epsilon > 0
limits: the counterexample shows epsilon-Nash should not be interpreted as a return-approximation of Nash equilibrium; this is a stated conceptual limitation, not a universal impossibility proof
statement: An epsilon-Nash equilibrium (Definition 7, Eq. 4.18) relaxes strict Nash equilibrium to allow at most epsilon improvement from unilateral deviation, but the authors give an explicit counterexample (Figure 4.2) in which an epsilon-Nash equilibrium's expected returns can be arbitrarily far from any real Nash equilibrium's returns, even when the Nash equilibrium is unique.

conditions: general-sum normal-form games with n agents; the recommendation policy is commonly known and each agent observes only its own recommended action
limits: the containment result is cited (Osborne and Rubinstein 1994), not proved in this text
statement: Correlated equilibrium (Definition 8, Eq. 4.19) generalizes Nash equilibrium by allowing agents' actions to be jointly correlated via a shared recommendation policy; the set of correlated equilibria contains the set of Nash equilibria, with Nash equilibrium being the special case where the joint recommendation policy factors into independent per-agent policies (Osborne and Rubinstein 1994).

conditions: non-repeated Chicken matrix game, specific correlated policy pi_c(L,L)=pi_c(S,L)=pi_c(L,S)=1/3, pi_c(S,S)=0

statement: In the Chicken matrix game, a correlated equilibrium exists that gives both agents an expected return of 5, exceeding the return (about 4.66 each) of the best symmetric Nash equilibrium reachable under independent policies, illustrating that allowing correlation can strictly improve on what independent (Nash) policies achieve.

conditions: general-sum games; welfare and fairness defined per Definitions 10-11

statement: Welfare optimality (maximizing the sum of agents' expected returns, Eq. 4.26) implies Pareto optimality (proof given by contradiction, p. 109), but the converse does not hold; fairness optimality (maximizing the product of agents' expected returns, Eq. 4.27, i.e. Nash social welfare) neither implies nor is implied by Pareto optimality.

statement: Computing an equilibrium satisfying an additional decision-problem property -- Pareto optimality, a minimum per-agent expected return, a minimum social welfare, or fixed action-support constraints -- is NP-hard (Gilboa and Zemel 1989; Conitzer and Sandholm 2008), whereas minimax solutions (via linear programming, Section 4.3.1) and correlated equilibria (via linear programming, Section 4.6.1) are both computable in polynomial time.

statement: Computing a Nash equilibrium (NASH) in general-sum non-repeated normal-form games is PPAD-complete: proven first for games with three or more agents (Daskalakis, Goldberg, and Papadimitriou 2006, 2009), then for exactly two agents (Chen and Deng 2006); the approximate epsilon-Nash version is PPAD-complete for certain bounds on epsilon, and the exact (epsilon=0) version is PPAD-complete for two-agent games.

statement: The PPAD-completeness of NASH (Section 4.11.2) establishes that no known efficient (polynomial-time) algorithm computes Nash equilibria for general games without exploiting additional structure or assumptions; it does not by itself say anything about the computational difficulty of the narrower or differently-scoped objectives used by non-equilibrium-seeking MARL methods, such as objectives built around skill discovery, intrinsic reward, or common-reward maximization rather than Nash-equilibrium computation.

statement: For any NoSDE game with a unique equilibrium joint policy, there exists another NoSDE game differing only in the reward functions, with its own unique equilibrium policy, such that the two games share identical equilibrium joint-action value functions for every agent, yet the two equilibrium policies yield different expected returns (value functions) for at least one agent.

statement: Deep Q-learning replaces the tabular Q-learning update with a neural network Q(s,a;θ) trained by minimizing the squared error between Q(s_t,a_t;θ) and a bootstrapped target y_t, where y_t = r_t if s_{t+1} is terminal and y_t = r_t + γ max_{a'} Q(s_{t+1},a';θ) otherwise (Equations 8.2–8.3, Algorithm 10).

statement: The book defines the 'deadly triad' (citing Sutton and Barto 2018; van Hasselt et al. 2018) as the combination of off-policy learning, function approximation, and bootstrapped targets, and states this combination 'can lead to unstable and diverging value estimates.'

statement: The book states that RL violates both parts of the i.i.d. assumption underlying most machine learning: consecutive experience samples are correlated because s_{t+1} and r_t are determined by the transition function conditioned on s_t and a_t, and the sampling distribution shifts as the policy changes; a replay buffer D storing past transitions, from which mini-batches are sampled uniformly at random (B ~ U(D)), is introduced to break these correlations (Algorithm 12 / DQN).

statement: DQN is stated to be 'prone to overestimation of action values' because the target uses max_{a'} Q(s_{t+1},a';θ); double deep Q-networks (DDQN) reduces this by decoupling greedy action selection (via the main network's arg max) from action-value evaluation (via the target network), per Equation 8.6.

limits: The textbook does not reproduce the Rainbow experiment itself; it cites Hessel et al. 2018 for the performance claim.
statement: The book states that combining DDQN, prioritized experience replay (Schaul et al. 2016), parameterized exploration noise (Fortunato et al. 2018), dueling value/advantage decomposition (Wang et al. 2016), and distributional value learning (Bellemare, Dabney, and Munos 2017) yields the Rainbow algorithm, 'shown to exhibit significantly higher performance than DQN across Atari games (Hessel et al. 2018).'

conditions: Policy gradient theorem (Sutton and Barto 2018) as stated by the authors; applies to episodic environments; requires a differentiable policy parameterization.
limits: Q^π(s,a) in the theorem must itself be approximated since it is not known a priori; the book notes DQN-style algorithms do not satisfy the on-policy requirement because they approximate the optimal value function via the Bellman optimality equation instead.
statement: The policy gradient theorem's expectation is defined under the state distribution Pr(s|π) and action distribution π(·|s;ϕ) of the current policy π being optimized; the book states this 'clearly illustrates the restriction that follows from the policy gradient theorem: the optimization of the parameterized policy is limited to on-policy data' and that data from any different policy π′ — including older versions of π obtained earlier in training — 'can not be used to update π following the policy gradient theorem.'

conditions: Requires full episode rollouts (updates occur after episode termination); on-policy Monte Carlo returns.
limits: High-variance gradients are stated as an explicit limitation of the base algorithm without a baseline.
statement: REINFORCE (Williams 1992) instantiates the policy gradient theorem with Monte Carlo estimates of episodic returns, minimizing L(ϕ) = -(1/T) Σ_t (Σ_{τ≥t} γ^{τ-t} r_τ) log π(a_t|s_t;ϕ) (Equations 8.15–8.16, Algorithm 13); the book states 'Monte Carlo return estimates have high variance, which leads to high variance of gradients and unstable training in REINFORCE' because returns depend on the entire episode's states and actions.

conditions: The baseline must be a function of state only (not of the action) for the derivation to hold.
limits: none
statement: The book derives (Equations 8.17–8.27) that subtracting any baseline b(s), defined only over the state s, from Q^π(s,a) in the policy gradient theorem leaves the expected gradient unchanged, because Σ_a b(s)∇_ϕπ(a|s;ϕ) = b(s)∇_ϕ Σ_a π(a|s;ϕ) = b(s)∇_ϕ 1 = 0; a state-value function V(s;θ), trained by minimizing L(θ)=(1/T)Σ_t(u_t - V(s_t;θ))², is given as a common baseline choice.

conditions: Requires a trained critic V(s;θ); the bootstrapped estimate uses one-step (or N-step) lookahead.
limits: Bias is explicitly acknowledged as the cost of bootstrapping; the book states 'we find that the trade-off of bias for lower variance often improves training stability' without a formal bound.
statement: Actor-critic algorithms use a critic V to compute bootstrapped return estimates (Equations 8.30–8.32) instead of full Monte Carlo returns; the book states this gives two benefits — updates from a single time step's experience rather than waiting for episode end, and lower variance than Monte Carlo returns — 'at a price of introduced bias, because the used value function might not (yet) approximate the true expected returns of states.'

conditions: Measured post hoc from 10,000 evaluation episodes collected with a policy trained for 100,000 time steps with N=5 in one specific environment.
limits: Single environment, single trained policy; the book presents this to illustrate the general bias-variance trade-off qualitatively, not as a quantitative law for other tasks.
statement: Using a critic trained with A2C (N=5) in the single-agent level-based-foraging task, the book reports that measured variance of N-step return estimates increases with N (approaching Monte Carlo variance at N=T) while measured bias decreases with N (approaching zero, the unbiased Monte Carlo case), shown for N∈{1,...,10} plus Monte Carlo in Figure 8.5.

conditions: Requires both actor π(·;ϕ) and critic V(·;θ) networks trained jointly (Algorithm 14).
limits: The book explicitly flags its Algorithm 14 as a simplification of the original A2C/A3C algorithm.
statement: Advantage actor-critic (A2C) estimates the advantage Adv(s,a) = Q(s,a) - V(s), approximated using the critic as Adv(s_t,a_t) = r_t - V(s_t;θ) if s_{t+1} terminal else r_t + γV(s_{t+1};θ) - V(s_t;θ) (Equation 8.36), and minimizes the actor loss L(ϕ) = -Adv(s_t,a_t) log π(a_t|s_t;ϕ) (Equation 8.38) jointly with a critic squared-error loss (Equation 8.40); the book denotes its presented pseudocode 'Simplified A2C' since the original A2C/A3C (Mnih et al. 2016) also uses multi-step returns and entropy regularization.

conditions: Applied as an additional term added to the actor loss; the original A2C/A3C uses it, while the book's 'Simplified A2C' (Algorithm 14) omits it by default.
limits: none
statement: Entropy regularization adds the negative policy entropy, -H(π(·|s;ϕ)) = Σ_a π(a|s;ϕ) log π(a|s;ϕ) (Equation 8.41), to the actor loss; the book states that maximizing entropy 'penalizes the policy for assigning a very high probability to any action' and 'discourages premature convergence to a suboptimal close-to-deterministic policy,' thereby incentivizing exploration.

conditions: The comparison is qualitative/conceptual, not a reported head-to-head experiment in this chapter.
limits: No empirical comparison of TRPO vs. PPO is presented in this section; the comparison is descriptive.
statement: The book contrasts trust region policy optimization (TRPO, Schulman et al. 2015), which 'constrains each optimization step... to a small trust region' but 'requires either solving a constrained optimization problem or computing a penalty term, which are both computationally expensive,' with PPO's clipped surrogate objective, described as computationally efficient.

conditions: ε is a hyperparameter bounding how far the updated policy's action probability may diverge from π_β; requires a critic for the advantage estimate (Equation 8.36).
limits: The book describes only the clipped-surrogate PPO variant in detail, noting Schulman et al. (2017) also propose a KL-divergence-penalty variant that it does not detail.
statement: PPO (Schulman et al. 2017, clipped-objective variant) computes an importance sampling ratio ρ(s,a) = π(a|s;ϕ)/π_β(a|s) (Equation 8.42) between the policy being optimized and the behavior policy that generated the data, and minimizes L(ϕ) = -min(ρ(s_t,a_t)·Adv(s_t,a_t), clip(ρ(s_t,a_t), 1-ε, 1+ε)·Adv(s_t,a_t)) (Equation 8.43, Algorithm 15); this clipping lets PPO reuse the same batch of data for N_e update epochs, unlike standard on-policy policy gradient methods that require freshly on-policy data for every update.

conditions: Small actor/critic networks (two layers, 32 hidden units), γ=0.99; REINFORCE learning rate 1e-3 without baseline; A2C/PPO learning rate 3e-4, N=5.
limits: Single fixed small-scale single-agent task; not a general ranking claim across environments.
statement: In the single-agent level-based-foraging task (Figure 8.3(a)), REINFORCE, A2C (N=5), and PPO (N=5, ε=0.2, N_e=4 epochs) are trained for 100,000 time steps across five seeds (Figure 8.6): REINFORCE 'learns to solve the task in most runs' but with 'high variance... all throughout training'; A2C and PPO with N-step returns 'reach the optimal performance across all runs within 60,000 time steps'; PPO 'is able to learn slightly faster than A2C, which can be explained by its optimization being able to use each batch of experiences multiple times.'

statement: Because 'on-policy policy gradient algorithms cannot make use of a replay buffer,' the book presents synchronous data collection (parallel environment instances, agent waits for all threads each step, Algorithm 16/Figure 8.7) and asynchronous training (each thread holds its own agent copy and environment, updates a shared central network, Figure 8.9) as the two techniques used instead to break correlations and obtain larger batches for on-policy algorithms.

conditions: γ=0.99, learning rate 1e-3, N-step returns with N=10, small actor/critic networks (two 32-unit layers); wall-clock training capped at five minutes.

statement: In a 12x12 level-based-foraging task requiring collection of two items, simplified A2C is trained for five minutes with K ∈ {1,4,16,64} synchronous environments (Figure 8.8): smaller K is comparably sample-efficient per time step but less stable (K=1 'does not converge to the optimal policy'), while larger K is more wall-clock efficient, though 'these benefits diminish with a growing number of synchronous environments' due to threads idling while waiting for the slowest thread.

statement: For partially observable environments, the book states that value functions and policies 'should be conditioned on the episodic history of observations, h_t = (o_0,...,o_t)'; rather than concatenating or zero-padding the growing history (called impractical, and for zero-padding 'not applicable to tasks with potentially infinite episodes'), it recommends using a recurrent neural network to process the history one observation at a time, with GRUs and LSTMs cited as the RNN architectures 'commonly used in deep RL.'

limits: the authors note this is a known challenge, not a proof of failure in all cases; independent learning 'often performs well in practice'
statement: In independent learning, each agent treats the other agents as part of a non-stationary component of the environment rather than modeling them explicitly; as other agents' policies change, the transition, observation, and reward functions perceived by each individual agent change too, which the authors state can lead to unstable learning and poor convergence, despite independent learning often performing well in practice.

conditions: applies when the application scenario allows privileged information to be shared only during training, not at deployment
limits: none stated in this passage
statement: Centralized training with decentralized execution (CTDE) is defined as training that may use centrally shared information (e.g. all agents' observation histories or the full state) to update agent policies, while each agent's deployed policy is conditioned only on its own local observation history, so it can be executed independently; the value function used during training is no longer needed at execution time.

conditions: applies to off-policy algorithms using a replay buffer under concurrent multi-agent learning
limits: illustrative example, not an empirical measurement; mitigations discussed include smaller buffers, importance-sampling reweighting (Foerster et al. 2017), hysteretic Q-learning, and leniency
statement: Off-policy independent learning with a replay buffer (e.g. IDQN) can retain stale experience: as illustrated by a chess example where agent 2 learns to counter agent 1's opening, agent 1's replay buffer continues to hold now-outdated transitions that overstate the old opening's value, which can delay agent 1 from abandoning the countered strategy.

conditions: fully decentralized training and execution
limits: none stated beyond the general independent-learning caveats
statement: IDQN (Algorithm 17) gives each agent i its own action-value network Q(.;theta_i), its own target network, and its own replay buffer D_i; each agent's DQN loss (Eq. 9.1) is computed only from that agent's own local observation history, action, and reward, with no information sharing between agents at training or execution time, though all agents' losses are optimized simultaneously.

conditions: applies to on-policy independent policy-gradient methods (REINFORCE, A2C, PPO) versus off-policy value-based methods with replay buffers
limits: stated as a qualitative advantage, not quantified
statement: On-policy independent algorithms such as REINFORCE are stated to be less susceptible to the replay-buffer staleness problem than off-policy algorithms like IDQN, because they always learn from experience generated under the most recent (current) policies of the other agents.

conditions: CTDE paradigm; critic is unused after training completes

statement: Lyu et al. (2023), as reported by the authors, show that a centralized critic should at minimum be conditioned on the agent's own observation history (otherwise it may be biased and unable to infer the policy it evaluates), and that additional centralized information can introduce higher variance into the policy gradient during training without improving theoretical convergence guarantees, though the authors note this theoretical result relies on an assumption -- convergence of critics to true value functions under current policies -- that often does not hold in deep-learning practice, and empirically added information sometimes still helps avoid local optima.

statement: Difference rewards (Eq. 9.14) approximate agent i's contribution to a common reward as the difference between the actual received reward and the reward agent i would have received under a chosen default action, holding other agents' actions fixed; the aristocrat utility (Eq. 9.15) avoids needing a default action by instead subtracting the expected reward agent i would receive under its current policy.

statement: The individual-global-max (IGM) property (Eq. 9.25) requires that, for all full histories, a joint action is a greedy action of the decomposed centralized action-value function if and only if each agent's component action is a greedy action of that agent's own individual utility function; the authors note that in some environments, particularly under partial observability, no decomposition satisfying IGM may exist because individual utilities can lack the information to discriminate joint histories with different true action values.

statement: The book reproduces a complete taxonomy of 78 structurally distinct, strictly ordinal 2x2 normal-form games (Rapoport and Guyer 1966), split into 21 no-conflict games (agents share the same most-preferred outcome) and 57 conflict games (agents disagree on it), with pure Nash equilibrium outcomes marked. The authors state this taxonomy is complete: no listed game can be produced from another via row/column/agent relabeling.

conditions: Grid size, number of agents/items, and skill-level assignment are all task parameters; levels can be randomized per episode.
limits: The equation defining the per-agent reward (Eq. 11.1, p. 354) falls in a chunk (B01-C0077) flagged equation_text_unreliable, so its extracted summation symbols should not be trusted; consult the source page for the exact formula.
statement: In level-based foraging (LBF), n agents act in a fully observable grid-world with a discrete action space {up, down, left, right, collect, noop}; a group of adjacent agents can jointly collect an item only if they all select collect and the sum of their skill levels meets or exceeds the item's level, so higher-level items require cooperation among a subset of agents while lower-level items can be collected individually. Each task fixes the number of agents as a configuration parameter.

conditions: A specific configuration of the LBF task family, not the default; illustrated for an 8x8 grid, 3 agents, 5 items in Figure 11.2(b).
limits: This is one specific LBF task configuration among many possible parameterizations; the book states LBF is flexible across degrees of cooperation, observability, and scale.
statement: LBF's 'forced cooperation' task variant assigns item levels such that every item in the environment requires all agents in the task to cooperate to collect it, in contrast to the default random-level variant where some items are individually collectible and agents may compete for them.

conditions: Task-dependent: observability, reward structure (competitive/cooperative/common-reward), and action type (discrete/continuous) vary by which MPE task is configured.
limits: none
statement: The multi-agent particle environment (MPE) contains 2D navigation tasks spanning competitive, cooperative, and common-reward objectives with both full and partial observability, and both discrete cardinal-direction and continuous velocity action options; named tasks include predator-prey, coordinated navigation (3 agents, 3 landmarks), and speaker-listener, the last of which requires a speaker agent to communicate a hidden landmark color to a listener agent via binary communication actions.

conditions: Team size and unit composition are fixed per task/map; SMAC always pits the learned team against a fixed built-in AI opponent, not another learned team.
limits: none
statement: In SMAC, all tasks are partially observable (agents see health/shield status of themselves and nearby units within a radius), the team is rewarded with a dense common reward for damage dealt/units defeated plus a win bonus, and it plays against a fixed built-in AI. The authors state the shared common reward makes credit assignment especially prominent because actions (e.g., destroying a unit early) have long-term consequences that are hard to disentangle under one shared signal, which the authors say makes value-decomposition methods particularly suitable for SMAC.

conditions: The overfitting concern and SMACv2/SMAClite findings are attributed to the cited external papers, not independently reproduced in this book.
limits: The transfer-degradation finding is reported secondhand from the cited SMAClite paper; the book does not restate the magnitude of degradation. Fixed-per-task starting locations should not be read as evidence that SMAC agents generalize across configurations.
statement: Each SMAC task fixes the starting locations of all units, which the authors state can cause agents to overfit to that specific configuration (e.g., learning to act in a fixed order irrespective of state) rather than learning generalizable policies; SMACv2 (Ellis et al. 2023, cited) was proposed to randomize unit types and starting locations across episodes to address this. SMAClite (Michalski, Christianos, and Albrecht 2023, cited) reimplements SMAC without the StarCraft II game, and the authors report SMAClite-trained agents transfer to SMAC with some performance degradation, i.e., SMAC is accurately but not perfectly modeled by SMAClite.

conditions: Applies to RWARE's default individual-reward, sparse-delivery-reward structure; observation range (partial observability) and warehouse layout/agent count are task parameters.
limits: The parameter/experience-sharing benefit is attributed to the cited 2020 paper's demonstration, not re-derived in this chapter.
statement: In RWARE, agents receive individual (not shared) positive rewards only upon successfully delivering a requested shelf, making rewards very sparse since delivery requires long, specific action sequences; the authors state this sparsity makes parameter and experience sharing (Section 9.7) particularly well suited to RWARE, as demonstrated by Christianos, Schäfer, and Albrecht (2020, cited).

conditions: Reward function and observation mode are both independently selectable settings of the environment; agent count depends on whether whole-team or per-player control is chosen.
limits: none
statement: Google Research Football (GRF) supports a multi-agent interface with either two agents (one controlling each whole team) or per-player agent control of a cooperating team (up to full 11 vs. 11) against a fixed built-in AI, offers two selectable reward functions (goal-only, or additionally shaped for possession/forward progress) and three observation modes (pixel, compressed global map, or a 115-value feature vector).

conditions: Player count is fixed per game instance at a value between two and five, chosen before play begins; it does not vary within a game.
limits: none
statement: Hanabi is a fully cooperative, turn-based card game for two to five players in which each player sees every other player's cards but not their own, and communication is restricted to a shared pool of eight information tokens spent on hints; the authors state (citing Bard et al. 2020) that agents must adopt implicit conventions beyond the literal hint content to succeed, making Hanabi relevant to cooperative self-play, ad hoc teamwork, and acting under imperfect information.

conditions: Cooking Zoo's task diversity depends on its parameterization; Carroll et al.'s environment is explicitly scoped as more limited in recipes/layouts.
limits: none
statement: Two Overcooked-style implementations are described: Cooking Zoo (Rother, Weisswange, and Peters 2023), which supports customizable agent count, layouts, recipes, rewards, and observation spaces and is described as well suited to studying generalization to new tasks; and Carroll et al.'s (2019) Overcooked, similar in observation/action space but limited to a small fixed set of recipes and five map layouts with less customization, whose distinguishing advantage is a publicly available human-gameplay dataset.

conditions: The co-player generalization protocol holds the task fixed and varies only the identity/behavior of background agents drawn from a pretrained population; task-generalization is a separate, distinct axis in the same collection.
limits: This is generalization to varying co-player identity within a fixed task and agent-count setting, not evidence about generalizing a single trained policy across different agent counts (variable N) within one task.
statement: Melting Pot (Leibo et al. 2021) is explicitly designed to test two distinct kinds of generalization: across tasks (via a diverse set of over 50 tasks differing in agent count, objectives, and dynamics) and across co-players (via a focal population trained on one task that, during evaluation, is paired with varying background agents sampled from pretrained policies), so that evaluation measures zero-shot generalization to unfamiliar co-player behavior rather than to a different task.

conditions: OpenSpiel's simultaneous-move support is stated as an additional capability beyond its primary turn-based focus.

statement: OpenSpiel (Lanctot et al. 2019) is described as focused on turn-based ('extensive-form') games, including classical games such as Backgammon, Bridge, Chess, Go, and Poker, while also supporting simultaneous-move games matching this book's own game models; environments mix full and partial observability but all specify discrete actions, observations, and states.
